How Marketing Services Are Priced: Five Fee Models

Strategy

In short: Marketing services are priced five ways: retainer, project fee, hourly or daily, percent of spend, and performance. Each rewards the provider for something different, so find what makes the fee go up and you have found the advice you will get.

Key points

  • Retainers reward keeping the relationship; the risk is scope drift.
  • Percent-of-spend fees carry the sharpest conflict of interest because the provider earns more when the answer is more.
  • Performance deals depend entirely on how outcomes are defined, measured and attributed, and who controls measurement.
  • Never accept a free proposal for anything past a short conversation.
  • Insist the next step is priced in the same proposal as the current one.

The fee structure in a marketing proposal is the most reliable predictor of the advice you will receive. Five models cover almost every arrangement, and each one pays the provider for a different thing.

The five models

Retainer. A fixed monthly fee for an ongoing scope of work. Rewards the provider for keeping the relationship. Good for continuous work, running programs, managing channels, producing a regular cadence of content, and for predictability on both sides. The risk is scope drift: the work quietly shrinks while the fee does not, or expands while the fee does not, depending on who is paying less attention.

Project fee. A fixed price for a defined deliverable with a defined end. Rewards the provider for finishing. Good for work with a clear scope: a diagnostic, a positioning exercise, a program built and handed over, a launch. The risk is the scope document: a vague one produces disputes about what "done" meant.

Hourly or daily. Payment for time. Rewards the provider for spending time. Good for truly unpredictable work where neither side can scope in advance, and for very short engagements. The risk is obvious: the model pays for slowness, and the client carries all the estimation risk.

Percent of spend. A fee calculated as a share of the media budget the provider manages. Rewards the provider for spending more. The historical standard for media agencies and the model with the sharpest conflict of interest: every recommendation about budget, channel, and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more."

Performance. Payment tied to outcomes: leads, customers, revenue, or a bonus above a threshold. Rewards the provider for results, in principle. In practice it depends entirely on how the outcome is defined, measured, and attributed, and on who controls the measurement. Pure performance deals also push the provider toward the easiest outcomes and away from anything slow, such as brand, content, or a channel that takes a quarter to work.

What to read in a proposal

Find the fee. Ask what makes it go up. That is what the provider is being paid to do.

A retainer goes up when the relationship lasts. A project fee does not go up at all, which is why providers who quote them care about scope. Hourly goes up with time. Percent of spend goes up with budget. Performance goes up with outcomes as defined in the contract, so read the definition.

Then ask what is not included. Every model has edges, and the profitable part of many engagements is the work that falls outside the original description.

The combination that tends to work

For most companies buying distribution work, the least conflicted structure is a project fee against a written scope for anything with an end, a flat retainer for anything ongoing, media fees stated in dollars per account rather than as a percentage, no provider fronting the media spend, and a performance component only where the outcome is defined in writing and measured in the client's own systems.

That is the structure we publish, and we publish it because the alternative, a menu of fee models chosen to suit each deal, leaves the client guessing what the advice is for.

Two rules for the buyer

Never accept a free proposal for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document, and the provider's cost of producing it is recovered somewhere in the engagement. A paid, scoped first step, priced low enough to be an easy decision, produces advice with a defined end and no obligation.

And insist that the next step be priced in the same proposal as the current one. A provider who will not say what the next engagement costs until the current one is finished is pricing on dependency.

lowob takeaway: Retainers pay for relationships, project fees for finishing, hourly for time, percent of spend for spending, and performance for outcomes as defined. Find what makes the fee go up, and you have found the advice you will get.

Common questions

What are the main ways marketing agencies charge?

Five models cover almost every arrangement: a monthly retainer, a fixed project fee, hourly or daily rates, a percent of media spend, and performance-based fees tied to outcomes.

Is percent-of-spend agency pricing a conflict of interest?

Yes, it is the model with the sharpest conflict: every recommendation about budget, channel and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more."

What is the best fee structure when hiring a marketing agency?

A project fee against a written scope for anything with an end, a flat retainer for ongoing work, media fees stated in dollars per account, no provider fronting media spend, and performance pay only where outcomes are defined in writing and measured in the client's own systems.

Should I accept a free marketing proposal?

No, not for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document whose cost is recovered somewhere in the engagement; a paid, scoped first step gives advice with a defined end.
